interactions.label: Why must glycine occupy every third position in the collagen alpha chain?

params.question: Why must glycine occupy every third position in the collagen alpha chain?

answers.text: Glycine's single hydrogen side chain is the only one small enough to fit the crowded centre of the triple helix

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Every third residue faces inward in the tight triple helix. Only glycine, with its lone hydrogen atom as a side chain, fits there. Even one bulkier substitution kinks the helix — the basis of osteogenesis imperfecta.

answers.text: Glycine forms covalent cross-links with hydroxyproline residues on adjacent chains

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Glycine does not form covalent cross-links. Collagen cross-links are formed by lysyl oxidase acting on lysine and hydroxylysine residues, not glycine.

answers.text: Glycine's negative charge attracts the sodium ions needed for fibril assembly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Glycine carries no net charge at physiological pH. Dense negative charges that attract sodium belong to glycosaminoglycan sulphate and carboxylate groups, not to collagen residues.

answers.text: Glycine provides the rigid ring structure that locks each chain in a left-handed helix

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The rigid pyrrolidine rings belong to proline and hydroxyproline, which lock each alpha chain into an extended left-handed helix. Glycine's role is size — fitting the crowded core.

overallFeedback.feedback: Every third residue faces the centre of the triple helix, and only glycine — whose side chain is a single hydrogen atom — is small enough to fit there.
Well done. Glycine's tiny side chain is the molecular key to the triple helix — any bulkier residue at the centre disrupts the helix and causes disease.

interactions.label: Which property distinguishes hyaluronic acid from all other glycosaminoglycans?

params.question: Which property distinguishes hyaluronic acid from all other glycosaminoglycans?

answers.text: It is the most heavily sulphated GAG, stored inside mast cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The most heavily sulphated GAG is heparin, which is stored in mast-cell granules. Hyaluronic acid is the opposite — it is completely unsulphated.

answers.text: It is unsulphated, not attached to a core protein, and synthesised at the plasma membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Hyaluronic acid breaks every rule that applies to other GAGs: no sulphate groups, no core protein (so it is not a proteoglycan), and it is synthesised at the plasma membrane rather than in the Golgi.

answers.text: It is found only in the cornea, where it maintains tissue transparency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Keratan sulphate, not hyaluronic acid, is a major GAG of the cornea. Hyaluronic acid is widely distributed in connective tissues and synovial fluid.

answers.text: It forms covalent desmosine cross-links with adjacent polysaccharide chains

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Desmosine cross-links are unique to elastin, not to any glycosaminoglycan. Hyaluronic acid is distinctive for lacking sulphation and core-protein attachment.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall what makes hyaluronic acid 'the odd one out': no sulphate, no core protein, and made at the plasma membrane — the opposite of a typical bottle-brush proteoglycan GAG chain.
Excellent. Hyaluronic acid is unsulphated, protein-free, plasma-membrane-synthesised, and exceptionally long — the exception to every GAG rule.

interactions.label: A lysosomal enzyme that fails to receive its mannose-6-phosphate tag in the cis-

params.question: A lysosomal enzyme that fails to receive its mannose-6-phosphate tag in the cis-Golgi will most likely be:

answers.text: Retained in the endoplasmic reticulum by the KDEL retrieval system

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. KDEL retrieval recovers soluble ER-resident proteins that escape to the Golgi. It does not act on lysosomal enzymes. Without their M6P tag, these enzymes continue along the default secretory route.

answers.text: Returned to the cytosol and degraded by the proteasome

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Proteasomal degradation via retrotranslocation is the fate of proteins that misfold in the ER. Untagged lysosomal enzymes fold normally — they simply lack the address label for lysosomal delivery.

answers.text: Secreted from the cell instead of reaching lysosomes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Without the M6P tag, the Golgi cannot sort the enzyme to lysosomes. It follows the default secretory pathway and is released from the cell — exactly the mechanism behind I-cell disease.

answers.text: Imported into mitochondria via an N-terminal transit peptide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Mitochondrial import requires a specific amphipathic transit peptide that lysosomal enzymes do not carry. Mitochondrial and lysosomal targeting are entirely separate pathways.

overallFeedback.feedback: Without a mannose-6-phosphate tag, the Golgi has no way to divert the enzyme to lysosomes. It follows the default pathway to the cell surface and is secreted — the basis of I-cell disease.
Exactly right. Mannose-6-phosphate is the essential lysosomal sorting signal — without it, even properly folded enzymes default to secretion.

interactions.label: Hurler and Hunter syndromes both store heparan and dermatan sulphate. Which feat

params.question: Hurler and Hunter syndromes both store heparan and dermatan sulphate. Which feature best distinguishes Hunter from Hurler syndrome?

answers.text: Hunter syndrome is autosomal recessive and causes corneal clouding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect — the features are swapped. Hurler syndrome is autosomal recessive with corneal clouding. Hunter syndrome has X-linked inheritance and a clear cornea.

answers.text: Hunter syndrome is X-linked recessive and characteristically spares the cornea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Despite storing the same GAGs, Hunter syndrome is X-linked recessive (affected males, carrier mothers) and leaves the cornea clear — the two classic distinguishing features from Hurler.

answers.text: Hunter syndrome primarily stores keratan sulphate and affects the skeleton

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Keratan sulphate storage with predominantly skeletal involvement and preserved intelligence describes Morquio syndrome. Hunter syndrome stores heparan and dermatan sulphate.

answers.text: Hunter syndrome mainly affects the brain with relatively mild somatic features

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Predominantly neurological involvement with mild somatic features describes Sanfilippo syndrome. Hunter syndrome causes coarse facies, hepatosplenomegaly, and joint stiffness along with its neurological effects.

overallFeedback.feedback: Hurler and Hunter share their GAG storage, but differ in two key ways: inheritance (autosomal recessive vs X-linked recessive) and corneal involvement (clouded vs clear).
Well done. X-linked inheritance and clear corneas — these two features separate Hunter from Hurler despite identical GAG storage.

interactions.label: The nine-month-old infant in the opening case has high plasma lysosomal enzymes

params.question: The nine-month-old infant in the opening case has high plasma lysosomal enzymes but no raised urinary glycosaminoglycans. Which mechanism best explains this combination?

answers.text: A deficiency of a single lysosomal hydrolase, as in a classical mucopolysaccharidosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A single hydrolase deficiency raises urinary GAGs for the specific substrate of that enzyme. This child has multiple elevated plasma enzymes — pointing to a global tagging defect, not a single enzyme loss.

answers.text: Absence of the enzyme that adds the mannose-6-phosphate tag, so all lysosomal enzymes are secreted

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In I-cell disease, the N-acetylglucosamine phosphotransferase that adds the M6P tag is deficient. All lysosomal enzymes lose their address label and are secreted — hence the high plasma levels — while lysosomes fill with undigested material.

answers.text: Defective PEX gene products preventing protein import into peroxisomes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. PEX gene mutations cause Zellweger syndrome, which presents in the newborn with profound hypotonia, seizures, and elevated very-long-chain fatty acids — a different clinical picture from this child's coarse features and raised plasma enzymes.

answers.text: A defective copper transporter causing failure of lysyl oxidase cross-linking

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Defective copper transport (ATP7A mutation) causes Menkes disease, with kinky hair, tortuous arteries, and low serum copper — not coarse facies with elevated plasma lysosomal enzymes.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key clue is multiple lysosomal enzymes elevated in plasma. This signals a global sorting failure — the M6P tagging enzyme is deficient, so all lysosomal enzymes are secreted instead of reaching lysosomes. This is I-cell disease.
Excellent. The hallmark combination — Hurler-like features plus high plasma enzymes minus raised urinary GAGs — points to a global M6P tagging failure: I-cell disease.
